---
title: "Soul Recognition"
author: "DK"
date: "2026-08-23"
categories: [recognition]
---

Face recognition has always been a helpful tool—a gift—in my life.

I can see someone I haven't seen in years, or even decades, and remember them.

Somehow, their features, expressions, and presence stay with me.

Names, on the other hand, are far more difficult to retain.

A skill that was already weak is fading with age, compounded by language variations and subtle differences in how names are translated or spelled across cultures.

I may have to start writing names down instead of committing them to mental RAM (random access memory).

I have come to realize that a face is a temporary visual marker, and a name is an earthly label.

Both are temporal—confined to this life and destined to wear and fade away.

What ties us together, in this life and beyond, is the shared experience of the soul.

![](images/20260825_195841.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

This truth became clear to me recently while attending a missionary homecoming in Sandy, Utah.

The couple, J and D, had just returned from serving the people of Ghana.

They had left for Africa at the urging of their neighbor, who was assigned to a mission there, trusting in a higher power that their preparations would come together in just four short months.

As I listened to their report, I wondered if I would see anyone I knew.

Afterward, a former coworker from three years ago walked by with her husband—an unexpected reunion.

\[Interestingly, I remembered her husband's name just minutes after we spoke.\]

Later at the gathering, I met the missionary’s mother, Arlene.

When I mentioned that I live near BYU, she shared that she and her late husband, Joe, had served at the BYU Jerusalem Center years ago—completing a work that Joe and his first wife had originally begun.

Later, Arlene extended that same devotion to the people of Armenia and Georgia.

As we spoke about mutual acquaintances at the Center, we were connecting at a level deeper than a casual visit.

We navigate this life using name recognition, visual memory, and practical associations with people, places, and companies.

![](images/20260824_081543.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

But the most vital tool we need is soul recognition.

Unlike names and faces, which belong to this world, soul identification is not man-made, nor is it confined to a database or labeled with metadata.

It is eternal, God-given, and nurtured through divine connection.

We refine this spiritual recognition whenever we carry out our God-given missions—whether those efforts are visible and public, or quiet and unseen.

The names and faces of people like Arlene, Joe, J, and D may never be featured on popular websites or carried by mainstream media outlets.

Their physical features will age, and their names may eventually be forgotten by the world.

But their work is captured in the hearts of families and communities in Jerusalem, Tbilisi, and Takoradi.

Long after temporal labels fade away, the worth of a soul remains—recognized, magnified, and remembered eternally by the One w ho sent us, and by those they served.
